title: Injecting Services Into Views and Action Methods
description: Use @inject in Razor views and [FromServices] on action methods to consume DI services exactly where they are needed.

terms.definition: A Razor directive that resolves a service from the DI container and makes it available as a property in the view.
An MVC attribute placed on an action method parameter to resolve it from the DI container instead of from the request body or route.
Configuration values injected into a view using @inject IOptions<T>, giving the view access to strongly typed settings.
The practice of resolving a service directly inside a Razor view rather than passing it from the controller.

data.text: Constructor injection on a controller is the most common DI pattern, but it isn't always the right tool. Sometimes only one action method needs a service, or a Razor view needs data that the controller didn't pass. ASP.NET Core provides two targeted alternatives: `[FromServices]` for action methods and `@inject` for views.
When only one action needs a service, add it as a parameter decorated with `[FromServices]`. The container resolves it at call time — the controller's constructor stays clean.

data.title: [FromServices] on a single action parameter
data.content: Resolving ProductSummary only for the Summary action — not injected into the constructor

data.title: When to use [FromServices]
data.text: Use [FromServices] when the dependency is needed by only one or a few actions. If most actions need it, prefer constructor injection to keep the contract explicit.
The `@inject` directive resolves a service directly inside a Razor view. It is commonly used for `IConfiguration`, `IOptions<T>`, or small services that render part of the page.

data.text: Passing Services From Controller to View

A cleaner alternative to `@inject` is to resolve the service in the controller and pass the result to the view via the model or ViewBag. This keeps the view free of DI concerns and is easier to unit test.

data.text: For quick access to raw configuration keys, inject `IConfiguration` directly. This is less type-safe than the options pattern but useful for one-off lookups.

data.title: Rules of thumb
items: Use constructor injection as the default — it makes dependencies explicit.
Use [FromServices] when only one or two actions need the service.
Use @inject sparingly — prefer passing data from the controller.
Never resolve services manually with new inside controllers or views.
Avoid injecting IConfiguration directly into views — use IOptions<T> instead for type safety.

data.title: Exercise: Inject the Right Way
data.description: Refactor a controller and view to use the most appropriate DI technique for each situation.
steps: A WeatherController needs IOptions<ApiSettings> for every action — inject it via the constructor.
A single Export action needs an IReportGenerator only for that action — use [FromServices].
A _Layout.cshtml needs the app name from IOptions<AppSettings> — use @inject.
A view shows a list of products passed from the controller — keep the view free of @inject.
data.expectedOutcome: A controller with constructor-injected shared services, [FromServices] on the one-off action, and @inject used only in the layout where the controller cannot easily pass the data.

data.title: DI in Views and Actions Checklist

items.text: I know when to use constructor injection vs [FromServices]
items.hint: Constructor = shared by all actions; FromServices = one action only

items.text: I can use @inject to bring a service into a Razor view
I can inject IOptions<T> into a view to read typed settings
I understand why passing data from the controller is often better than @inject
I can read configuration with IConfiguration as a fallback

items.question: Is [FromServices] the same as constructor injection?
items.answer: The result is the same — the service comes from the DI container. The difference is scope: [FromServices] resolves per action call, constructor injection resolves once per controller instance.

items.question: Can I @inject a scoped service into a view?
items.answer: Yes. Razor views run within the HTTP request scope, so Scoped services are available. The same rules apply: do not use Scoped services inside Singletons.

items.question: Should I inject services into views or pass them from the controller?
items.answer: Prefer passing from the controller. It keeps views simpler and makes controllers easier to unit test. Use @inject for layout-level concerns or read-only configuration.

items.question: Can I use @inject inside a partial view?
items.answer: Yes. @inject works in any Razor file — views, partials, layouts, and view components. Each file resolves its own injection independently.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use constructor injection as the default — it makes dependencies explicit and testable.
Use [FromServices] when only one action needs a service — keeps the constructor lean.
Use @inject in views sparingly, mainly for configuration or layout-level data.
Prefer IOptions<T> over raw IConfiguration string lookups everywhere.
The goal is always the same: the right service, in the right place, with the least coupling.
data.takeaway: DI gives you many injection points. Choose the narrowest one that fits your use case to keep your code clean and testable.
